level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: print and println behave the same (no newline difference). Right rule: println(s) prints s and then ends the line, but print(s) does not, so print("a"); print("b"); gives ab on one line.

Points to LT (output appears in the order the output calls execute, with a line break only after println). An uneven trace drops a repeated value, puts output lines out of order, or adds line breaks after print on some calls. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
wrong rule: printf() ends the line like println(). Right rule: printf() adds no newline. Put \n (or %n) in the format string to end the line.

wrong rule: An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once. Right rule: Every expression in the output is printed, so System.out.println(y + " " + x + " " + y) with x=6, y=9 prints 9 6 9.
Switching System.out.print/println to StdOut.print/println keeps the output. Changing println to print keeps every character but removes the line break, so lines join.

wrong rule: Any conversion code (%d, %f, %s) works with any argument type. Right rule: The conversion must fit the argument's type (%s accepts any type). printf("%12d", Math.PI) or printf("%4.2f", 512) throws IllegalFormatConversionException at run time.

wrong rule: %2.4f prints two digits before the decimal point and four after. Right rule: The first number is the width of the whole field. %7.2f means 7 characters in total, with 2 digits after the decimal point.
wrong rule: printf() ends the line like println(). Right rule: printf() adds no newline. Put \n (or %n) in the format string.

Points to LT (specifiers are paired with arguments left to right, and the other characters pass through). An uneven trace pairs a specifier with the wrong argument, drops the literal text between specifiers, or pads on the wrong side on some fields. (here mixing in: "Any conversion code (%d, %f, %s) works with any argument type")

wrong rule: A result printed with many decimal places must be accurate to those places. Right rule: Printing precision is only formatting. A value printed to many places can still be inaccurate, and ensuring accuracy is the hard part.
Changing the precision changes only the printed digits, not the stored value. Changing the width changes only the padding. A width smaller than the converted text is ignored, so nothing is truncated.
